name: Cloudera, Inc. (including Hortonworks)
subcategory: Hadoop / big-data platform; hybrid data cloud
key_takeaway: Cloudera and Hortonworks are the Hadoop era's natural experiment in degrees of openness. Both IPO'd, neither thrived alone, they merged, the combined firm closed distribution rather than the licence, and private equity took it private in 2021. The Apache projects outlived both companies' independence.

name: Cockroach Labs, Inc.
subcategory: distributed SQL database (CockroachDB)
key_takeaway: Cockroach Labs shows that a database company can move from Apache to nearly proprietary with little community backlash when the project lacks a large independent contributor base or a hyperscaler with motive to fork. The cost is that it now competes as a proprietary vendor against Apache-licensed rivals (YugabyteDB, TiDB) and Postgres itself, with no public exit and a valuation last set at the 2021 peak.

name: Confluent, Inc. (an IBM company since 2026)
subcategory: data streaming platform (Apache Kafka)
key_takeaway: Confluent shows a middle path: keep the engine at a neutral foundation, monetize a cloud service and proprietary or source-available extras. It avoided the Elastic/Redis-style fork, grew to $1.17B in revenue, and was bought by IBM for ~$11B in March 2026. Together with HashiCorp, it shows IBM consolidating open-source-origin infrastructure companies, after Red Hat, as a strategy for enterprise AI.

name: Elastic N.V. (formerly Elasticsearch BV)
subcategory: search and analytics engine (Elasticsearch, Kibana)
forks: OpenSearch (and OpenSearch Dashboards), forked from Elasticsearch/Kibana 7.10.2, first released April 2021
key_takeaway: Elastic is the canonical relicense-fork-reversal story. Closing the licence protected Elastic Cloud from AWS resale, but it handed AWS the moral high ground and a permanent, foundation-governed fork that splits the ecosystem. Three years later Elastic re-added an OSI licence (AGPL), keeping SSPL/ELv2 alongside. The company stayed public and growing throughout, so the closing was not fatal, but it permanently lost sole control of the search-engine standard it created.

name: Grafana Labs (formerly Raintank)
subcategory: observability (Grafana, Loki, Mimir, Tempo, Pyroscope, k6)
key_takeaway: Grafana Labs is the main counter-example in this group: it chose an OSI copyleft licence over a source-available one, avoided any fork, and kept compounding its private valuation (over $6B in 2024). Elastic (2024) and Redis (2025) later re-added AGPL themselves, which makes Grafana's 2021 choice look like where the relicensing wave settled.

name: HashiCorp, Inc. (an IBM company since 2025)
subcategory: infrastructure automation (Terraform, Vault, Consul, Nomad, Packer, Vagrant)
forks: OpenTofu (Terraform fork from 1.5.7, accepted by the Linux Foundation 2023-09-20; CNCF Sandbox 2025-04-23) and OpenBao (Vault fork, started 2023-11-09 under LF Edge)
key_takeaway: HashiCorp is the case where relicensing came late in the company's life and preceded a sale. The BSL change likely made HashiCorp a cleaner asset for an acquirer, and IBM bought it within about 18 months, even though IBM engineers had led the open Vault fork. The open-source community kept its own copy of Terraform (OpenTofu, now in CNCF), so the open standard survives outside the vendor.

name: MariaDB (MariaDB plc / MariaDB Corporation and the MariaDB Foundation)
subcategory: relational database (MySQL fork)
key_takeaway: MariaDB exists because MySQL changed hands: it is a founder-led fork to keep the code under community control, backed by a nonprofit foundation. Its company struggled (SPAC listing, then a roughly $37M private-equity take-private) while the GPL server persists, separating the robustness of the code from that of the company. It also wrote the Business Source License used across the later relicensing wave.

name: MongoDB, Inc. (formerly 10gen)
subcategory: database (document / NoSQL)
key_takeaway: MongoDB is the clearest case of an open-source-origin company that closed its license and still kept growing: SSPL protected its managed-service business from cloud resale, and the market rewarded it with roughly a 20x rise from its IPO valuation. But closing the license did not remove competition, it moved it to the API layer, where the hyperscalers now back an MIT-licensed, foundation-governed alternative. For an openness study, MongoDB shows that a strong first-party cloud product, not the license, is what captures value, while openness mainly bought the early adoption.

name: Neo4j, Inc. (formerly Neo Technology)
subcategory: graph database
forks: PureThink's redistribution of Neo4j Enterprise with the Commons Clause removed
key_takeaway: Neo4j fought a fork of its relicensed code in court rather than in the market, and won, the opposite of OpenSearch or Valkey, where hyperscaler backers made forks durable. Closing Enterprise did not dent growth: about $550M raised, a $2.2B valuation and over $200M in revenue by 2024, with IPO preparation reported.

name: Redis Inc. (formerly Garantia Data, then Redis Labs)
subcategory: in-memory database / cache
forks: Valkey (from Redis 7.2.4, BSD-3-Clause), announced 2024-03-28 under the Linux Foundation
key_takeaway: Redis shows the limits of relicensing when the hyperscalers are your biggest distribution channel: the moment the core closed, they forked it into a neutral foundation and made the fork their default. Redis Inc. still grew past $300M ARR, but it has not IPO'd and secondary markets value it below its 2021 $2B round. The reversal to AGPL after antirez returned suggests the company concluded that the open-source label mattered more for developer adoption than the licence protection did.

name: Tiger Data (Timescale, Inc. d/b/a Tiger Data)
subcategory: time-series and analytics database (PostgreSQL extension)
key_takeaway: Tiger Data shows the 'extension' strategy: build on a community-governed open project (PostgreSQL), keep the core OSI-licensed, and restrict only cloud resale of add-ons. It avoided the fork dynamics of Elastic and Redis and reached unicorn status in 2022, then rebranded as Tiger Data in June 2025; no newer valuation was confirmed.

name: Airbyte, Inc.
subcategory: data integration (ELT connectors)
key_takeaway: Airbyte is the fast-closing case in this group: born MIT in 2020, ELv2 by 2021, a $1.5B valuation the same year, and then a long gap without new priced funding while bigger rivals merged. Openness bought rapid adoption; restriction came early to fend off cloud resellers, and the company's fate now depends on monetizing the cloud product.

name: Anaconda, Inc.
subcategory: Python/R data-science distribution and package repository; enterprise AI platform
forks: conda-forge (community channel) and Miniforge are the usual alternatives
key_takeaway: Anaconda is a cautionary case for scientific software: a company built on community open-source (NumPy/SciPy lineage) monetized by restricting access to the convenience layer (repository and installer) rather than the code, which shifted costs onto universities. Its 2025 raise at $1.5B and 2026 AI acquisitions show investors now value it as an enterprise AI platform rather than as a science tool.

name: Automattic Inc.
subcategory: web publishing (WordPress.com, WooCommerce, Jetpack, Tumblr)
key_takeaway: Automattic shows that a fully GPL product with weak neutral governance can turn a free-rider complaint into a governance crisis: the code stayed open, but the steward used trademarks and the plugin directory as leverage, leading to litigation (2024-2025) and a 2026 boardroom fight. Openness built a $7.5B (2021) company; personal control of the commons put it at risk.

name: Databricks, Inc.
subcategory: data lakehouse / data + AI platform
key_takeaway: Databricks is the strongest case for the academic-spin-out, foundation-governed open-core model: the founders gave Spark to the ASF, kept the commercial value in a managed cloud service, and became the most valuable company in this group (~$190B, Aug 2026) without ever relicensing to a restrictive licence. AI demand, not the open-source projects alone, explains the 2025-2026 valuation surge.

name: dbt Labs, Inc. (formerly Fishtown Analytics; now 'Fivetran + dbt Labs')
subcategory: analytics engineering / SQL data transformation
key_takeaway: dbt Labs turned a consultancy's open-source tool into an industry standard and a $4.2B (2022) valuation, then consolidated with Fivetran rather than IPO. It shows how a permissive, community-defined standard can create large value for the ecosystem while the originating company's standalone outcome is merger rather than independence.

name: GitHub, Inc.
subcategory: code hosting / developer platform / AI coding (Copilot)
key_takeaway: GitHub is the clearest case of a closed platform built on top of the open-source commons: openness in the ecosystem, not in the product, generated its value, and AI (Copilot) became its growth engine after acquisition. Its 2025 absorption into Microsoft CoreAI shows the commons' central infrastructure is now controlled by a big-tech AI strategy.

name: Hugging Face, Inc.
subcategory: open ML model/dataset hub and libraries
key_takeaway: Hugging Face is the strongest evidence in this group that openness can create outsized market value in the AI era: a small, open-core company became the commons' infrastructure and sold to Nvidia for $12.93B (Sep 2026). The trade-off is governance: the open AI ecosystem's main hub is moving from an independent startup to the dominant hardware vendor.

name: MuleSoft, LLC (formerly MuleSource; owned by Salesforce)
subcategory: integration platform / API management (iPaaS)
key_takeaway: MuleSoft is the 'open-source on-ramp' case: a community project (2003) became open core, then a proprietary platform that IPO'd (2017) and sold to Salesforce for $6.5B (2018). The open edition was archived in 2026, illustrating how openness can fade once a big-company parent controls the product.

name: NGINX, Inc. (acquired by F5)
subcategory: web server / reverse proxy / load balancer
key_takeaway: NGINX shows the 'ubiquitous but under-monetized' pattern: the most-used web server earned its company a modest exit, and corporate stewardship under F5 led core developers to fork (freenginx, Angie). Openness made the code robust against both the Rambler ownership claim and F5's priorities, but not the company's independence.

name: PostHog, Inc.
subcategory: product analytics / all-in-one product platform
key_takeaway: PostHog is a capital-efficient open-core startup: about $194M raised, profitable on cash flow, and valued at ~$1.4B (Oct 2025) within six years, with an MIT core and a fully FOSS mirror. It shows that clear separation of open and proprietary code (ee/ directory, posthog-foss) can avoid licence controversy while the business shifts to SaaS.

name: Supabase, Inc.
subcategory: Postgres development platform / backend-as-a-service
key_takeaway: Supabase is the clearest AI-era counterexample to relicensing: a level-3, Apache-2.0 company that grew from founding (2020) to a $10B pre-money valuation (Jun 2026) by being the open, Postgres-based backend that AI coding tools default to. Its risk is concentration on the AI app boom, not openness.

name: DeepSeek
subcategory: frontier open-weights LLMs (V3/V4, R1) and low-cost API
key_takeaway: DeepSeek is the strongest evidence in this group that open weights can shift market structure: an MIT-licensed model from a 2023 hedge-fund spin-off moved hundreds of billions in market value, prompted Sam Altman to say OpenAI needed 'a different open source strategy' (Jan 2025), before its Apache-2.0 gpt-oss release (Aug 2025), and fed Meta's rethink and still produced a $52-70B private valuation. Its openness is about weights and licence, not data, and its biggest risks are geopolitical rather than commercial. For the study, it shows that a permissive licence can be a competitive weapon for

name: xAI (X.AI Holdings Corp.; subsidiary of SpaceX since Feb 2026)
subcategory: frontier LLMs (Grok) and consumer chatbot integrated with X
key_takeaway: xAI is the 'open-washing' contrast case: its founder sued OpenAI over abandoning its non-profit founding mission (Musk v. Altman, lost May 2026; see openai.json), yet xAI is closed at the frontier, releasing older weights under a licence that blocks the most valuable reuse (training other models). Its trajectory from 2023 founding to a $250B acquisition price shows that a frontier lab's market value can be built almost entirely without openness. For the study, it shows why the licence of an open-weights release matters as much as the release itself.

name: Formlabs Inc.
subcategory: professional SLA/SLS 3D printers and materials (closed comparator)
key_takeaway: Formlabs is the US closed comparator that scaled: an MIT Media Lab spin-out with about $249M in disclosed venture rounds, a $2B 2021 valuation, about $250M 2025 revenue and 750 staff, larger than every open desktop-printer maker in this group. It suggests that in professional additive manufacturing, proprietary integration of printer, materials and software captured more value than open designs did, with selective interface openness used as a growth tool.

name: MakerBot Industries, LLC
subcategory: desktop FFF 3D printers (now UltiMaker's education brand)
key_takeaway: MakerBot is the canonical 'open, then closed, then absorbed' arc: openness and community created the brand and the exit value, and closing (just before the Stratasys deal) traded community goodwill for proprietary control that did not prevent rapid value destruction. Within seven years of the $403M deal it was folded into Ultimaker as a minority-owned brand.

name: SiFive, Inc.
subcategory: RISC-V processor IP and fabless semiconductor
key_takeaway: SiFive is the clearest example of open-standard, closed-implementation hardware: the open RISC-V ISA created the market, while SiFive's own open-source platform was archived once it had served as a launch vehicle. It shows that an open specification can support a multi-billion-dollar US company, but the money comes from proprietary IP, long timelines and repeated large VC rounds, not from selling open designs.

name: Benchling, Inc.
subcategory: cloud R&D informatics SaaS (ELN, molecular biology, registry, LIMS) for biotech
key_takeaway: Benchling is the closed-SaaS benchmark for lab software. It is founder-led (MIT/YC 2012), raised about $406M, was valued at $6.1B at the 2021 peak and has about 810 employees. It has never open-sourced its product, and its free academic tier did the community-building job that open source does for others. The lack of any public valuation, IPO or reported down round since 2021 makes its current value unknown. Fetched sources could not confirm 2023-2026 restructuring.

name: CuspAI (Cusp AI Limited)
subcategory: AI materials-discovery platform ('AI Materials Foundry') for semiconductors, energy and chemicals
key_takeaway: CuspAI, Cambridge UK, founded 2024 by Chad Edwards and Max Welling, had raised over $650M by late 2026, among the largest sums in AI for materials. It has released nothing open, and its edge is a partner ecosystem combining licensed crystallographic databases, Wiley literature, semiconductor and chemicals companies and Meta's open models. It is the archetype of consuming open and licensed scientific data while keeping outputs proprietary.

name: Lila Sciences, Inc.
subcategory: 'scientific superintelligence' + autonomous AI Science Factories (life science, chemistry, materials, energy)
key_takeaway: Lila Sciences is the Flagship version of the 2025-2026 AI-for-science boom. It raised $550M in seven months of 2025, was valued above $1.3B with NVIDIA backing, and makes heavy physical-science claims (green-hydrogen catalysts, carbon-capture sorbents), all on proprietary instruments and data. It publishes papers but releases no models, data or code, so it shares results, not the means to reproduce them.

name: Opentrons Labworks, Inc.
subcategory: lab automation / low-cost liquid-handling robots
key_takeaway: Opentrons is the canonical open-hardware lab-automation test case, and its arc is 'open to enter, close the hardware to scale': the open OT-One won early users cheaply, but revenue came from a closed-hardware OT-2/Flex whose open Apache-2.0 API is the remaining open asset and the reason it dominates academic self-driving-lab builds. Its valuation fell about 91% from the 2021 SoftBank round to the 2025 Series D, a COVID boom-and-bust rather than a verdict on openness. In 2026 it repositioned as 'open, AI-native' infrastructure connecting AI to the wet lab, marketing 'open' as API access rather

name: Markforged Holding Corporation (MarkForged, Inc.)
subcategory: composite (continuous carbon fibre) FFF and bound-metal 3D printers, 'Digital Forge' platform
key_takeaway: Markforged is a SPAC-era closed-hardware story: about $137M of venture money and a ~$2.1B SPAC valuation in 2021, then a 1-for-10 reverse split, a patent loss, a $116M take-private by Nano Dimension in 2025 and a $42.5M resale to Stratasys in 2026. Its proprietary, cloud-tied printers changed hands twice in thirteen months, which is the vendor-continuity risk a lab takes on when it buys closed AM hardware.

name: LangChain, Inc.
subcategory: LLM application / agent frameworks plus agent observability, evaluation and deployment platform (LangSmith)
key_takeaway: LangChain is the AI-era template of a permissive framework plus a proprietary SaaS: MIT from day one with no relicensing, the paid product (LangSmith) kept outside the open repo from launch and made framework-agnostic, and $460M raised at a $3B valuation (2026-11-13). It shows open source still works as a go-to-market in the AI era when the business is a hosted, closed companion product rather than the open code itself.

name: Modular Inc.
subcategory: AI compiler, programming language (Mojo) and inference platform (MAX, Modular Cloud)
key_takeaway: Modular is an AI-era case of 'closed first, open later': a language and inference stack built under proprietary licences that a chip maker (Qualcomm) bought for a reported $3.9B in July 2026, after which the Mojo compiler went Apache-2.0 and MAX became source-available. The money comes from hosted inference and the strategic value of a cross-hardware software layer, not from the licence; MAX still stops short of OSI open source.

name: Nous Research
subcategory: open-weight model fine-tunes (Hermes), decentralised training (Psyche), open-source agent (Hermes Agent)
key_takeaway: Nous Research is the community-origin case in this group: open fine-tunes and crypto-funded decentralised training attracted capital, but the licence that mattered commercially was MIT on an agent framework, sold as a hosted service ($20-$200/month) with an enterprise edition planned. Its biggest model weights, as Llama derivatives, stayed at level 1.

name: Together Computer, Inc. (Together AI)
subcategory: AI cloud: open-model inference API, fine-tuning/post-training and GPU clusters
key_takeaway: Together AI shows the most common AI-era pattern in this group: advocate open models, publish research openly, and sell proprietary compute. It never relicensed anything; instead the product moved from 'open models + cloud' (2023) to a capital-intensive GPU cloud with 500+ MW of commitments (2026), so its fortunes depend on open-weight models staying good, not on its own code being open.

name: Weights & Biases, Inc.
subcategory: ML experiment tracking / MLOps and LLMOps platform
key_takeaway: Weights & Biases shows the AI-era 'open client, closed service' model: an MIT SDK spread through the ML community, but the value captured was in the proprietary hosted platform, which a GPU cloud (CoreWeave) bought for ~$1.7B in 2025 to move up the stack from compute to developer tools. It is an exit for a mostly closed product, not evidence that an open-source licence itself was the business.
